Assail means to attack something or someone — but not just any ordinary attack. The word carries a strong sense of force, intensity, and being overwhelmed. Think of it as being hit hard, either physically or non-physically, often all at once and from multiple directions.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Physical Attack (less common today)

In its most literal sense, to assail someone means to physically attack them with great violence and force. This usage is old-fashioned and mostly found in literature, historical writing, or formal contexts.

The enemy soldiers assailed the castle walls from all sides.

The crowd assailed the guard, pushing and striking him violently.

You would rarely hear someone say "he assailed me" in casual modern conversation to describe a street fight — you'd more likely say "he attacked me." But in novels, news writing, or formal prose, assail still appears this way.

2. Non-Physical / Figurative Attack (very common today)

This is where assail truly lives in modern English. It is used constantly to describe situations where someone — or something — is overwhelmed, bombarded, or hit hard by something non-physical. The "attacker" here is not necessarily a person; it can be an emotion, a smell, a sound, a question, a criticism, a memory, or even bad news.

This is the sense you will encounter most often, so pay close attention here.

A. Being overwhelmed by emotions or mental states

When strong feelings hit you suddenly and powerfully — especially unwanted ones — we say you are assailed by them.

She was assailed by guilt the moment she told the lie.

Walking into his old home, he was assailed by memories of his childhood.

He was assailed by doubt just before the exam began.

The feeling doesn't creep up slowly — it hits you, sometimes all at once.

B. Being bombarded with questions, criticism, or words

When people fire questions at you aggressively, or criticize you heavily, they assail you.

The journalist was assailed by reporters the moment she stepped out of the building.

The politician was assailed with harsh criticism from all sides after his speech.

She walked into the meeting and was immediately assailed with questions she wasn't prepared for.

C. Being hit by a strong sensory experience (smell, sound, noise)

When a powerful smell, noise, or sensation strikes you the moment you enter a place, writers often say it assails you. This is vivid, expressive language.

The moment he opened the fridge, a terrible smell assailed him.

As she stepped into the market, the noise and chaos assailed her senses.

A wave of heat assailed them as they stepped off the plane.
What Makes "Assail" Different from Simply Saying "Attack"?

This is important. "Attack" is broader and more neutral. "Assail" is more specific and more intense. Here's how they differ:

  • Assail implies being overwhelmed. It's not just one small hit — it suggests something coming at you with full force, often from multiple directions or all at once.
  • Assail is more formal and literary. You'd see it in a newspaper, a novel, or a speech — not typically in casual text messages.
  • Assail works where "attack" sounds too weak. If someone is flooded with self-doubt, you wouldn't say "he was attacked by doubt" — that sounds odd. But "he was assailed by doubt" sounds natural and precise.
  • The victim often feels helpless. Being assailed suggests you didn't see it coming, or that the force is too strong to easily resist.
A Key Grammar Pattern to Know

The most common grammatical pattern is:

Someone/something was assailed by [something intense]

This passive form ("was assailed by") is extremely common, especially in the figurative sense. It puts the focus on the person being overwhelmed, not on who or what is doing the overwhelming.

He was assailed by fear.
She was assailed by a flood of memories.
The government was assailed by public outrage.

You can also use it in the active form:

Doubts assailed him throughout the night.
The smell of smoke assailed her nostrils.
Critics assailed the new policy.

Assail is a strong, serious, and somewhat formal word. It is not dramatic in a sensational way — it is measured but forceful. Writers use it when they want to show that something is hitting a person hard and with real impact, whether that's a wave of emotion, a barrage of criticism, or an overwhelming sensory experience. It paints a picture of something powerful crashing into a person all at once.
A Quick Mental Picture to Remember It

Imagine you're walking into a room, and the moment you open the door, ten people immediately start shouting questions at you, a wave of heat hits your face, and a sharp smell fills your nose — all at the same time. That feeling of being hit from everywhere at once, overwhelmed and caught off guard? That is what it means to be assailed.
